message.content: A mechanical water pump moves water uphill by converting rotational or kinetic energy into hydraulic pressure through a sealed chamber and moving parts. In a common piston pump, a crank or motor drives a piston back and forth inside a cylinder; as the piston retracts, it creates a partial vacuum that opens an intake valve and draws water up from a lower source through a suction pipe. When the piston advances, it closes the intake valve and forces water through an outlet valve into a delivery pipe, increasing its pressure enough to push it upward against gravity. Rotary pumps use spinning impellers or gears to trap water between vanes or teeth and fling it outward into a volute, where velocity converts to pressure that drives flow through a discharge line to a higher elevation. By repeatedly trapping, pressurizing, and expelling small volumes of water, the pump overcomes the weight of the water column and elevation difference, delivering a continuous stream uphill as long as the mechanical input sustains the cycle and seals prevent backflow.
